items.readable_text:
Content:
In addition to using the formula
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1)d]
to compute the terms of an arithmetic sequence, we can also use it to compute the index of a particular term. The index of a term is simply the value of [MATH: n] corresponding to that term.

Content:
To illustrate, suppose we're given the following arithmetic sequence:

Content:
[MATH: 1, \: 4, \: 7, \: 10, \ \ldots, \: 28, \: \ldots]

Content:
If the first term is [MATH: 1,] the second term is [MATH: 4,] the third term is [MATH: 7,] and so on, then what term gives the value [MATH: 28?] In other words, what value of [MATH: n] gives [MATH: a_n=28?]

Content:
Since [MATH: a_1=1] and [MATH: d=3,] we can construct the formula for the [MATH: n]th term as follows:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1)d; = 1 + (n − 1)(3); = 1 + 3n − 3; = 3n − 2]

Content:
Now we can solve for the value of [MATH: n] that gives [MATH: a_n=28,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= 3n − 2; 28|= 3n − 2; 30|= 3n; 10|= n]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: 28] is the [MATH: 10]th term of the sequence.

[MATH: a_{n+1} = a_n + 12, \quad a_1 = 3,\quad n\geq 1,] what is the index of the term [MATH: 255?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We will convert the recursive formula to an explicit formula and then solve for the value of [MATH: n] such that [MATH: a_n=255.]

The recursive rule for an arithmetic sequence takes the form [MATH: a_{n+1} = a_n +{\color{black}d}.]

In the given formula, we have [MATH: d={\color{black}12}.] We are also told that [MATH: a_1={\color{black}3},] so we can write the explicit formula as follows:

[MATH: a_{n}|= a_{1} + (n − 1)d; = 3 + (n − 1)(12); = 3 + 12n − 12; = 12n − 9]

Now, we solve for the value of [MATH: n] such that [MATH: a_n=255\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: a_{n}|= 12n − 9; 255|= 12n − 9; 264|= 12n; (264)/(12)|= n; 22|= n]

Therefore, [MATH: 255] is the [MATH: 22]nd term of the sequence.
